If you're wearing a hat and have dirt on your mouth, chances are you're staying in a cottage . That's because cottages are usually in the countryside, which means you're likely spending time out in the garden, with a hat on and dirt all over your mouth. You know, your average cottage experience. And hey, this radical even kind of looks like a cottage.
You see a leaf ear, better known as an elf ! Elves are just humans who have ears that are pointy like leaves.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means same .

If you look closely and carefully, sometimes you can see some private legs in winter. Whose legs? Spider legs! It's too cold for them in winter, so they hide in cracks and crevices, but sometimes you can see their little leggies sticking out anyway.

Tie a thread to yourself whenever you take the blame for someone. This marks your achievement . Your achievement in blame-taking, I guess. Isn't it a great achievement to selflessly shield others from blame? Of course it is! So these little blame-threads are symbols of your achievement. Hints Pretty soon your fingers, toes, and whole body are covered in threads, for all your innumerable achievements. Think back on those achievements, on all those times you took the blame for someone. You're just so, so selfless. What a good person you are. Ahh, it feels good to be good.
readingMnemonic: But your latest achievement is covering yourself in these threads and everyone thinking it's sexy ( せき ). The newspapers and fashion mags can't get enough of your sexy style. See? If you're a good person, people will think your achievements are sexy. Hints Imagine setting this sexy thread-based fashion trend. You're named the sexiest person alive and everyone dresses like spools of thread to copy you. But the achievements to match? Well, only you have those.

meaningMnemonic: Take some alcohol and put a spider in it to make acid . Spiders have a little acid in them already, but if you want something really potent, smash one up in some whiskey to make a deadly acid that'll rip through anything. Hints Imagine crushing up some spiders into alcohol. Watch it turn green. It's going to eat through the beaker! Quick, do something!
readingMnemonic: You're trying to find a container for this acid when San ta-san ( さん ) bursts through your wall. He frowns down at you. You're on the naughty list now. You killed spiders AND made dangerous acid? Ooooh you're in trouble. Hints It's Christmas morning. Instead of gifts, Santa-san just throws a piece of charcoal at your face. Feel the charcoal smash into your face and explode into acid, burning you. Santa-san runs away laughing. Ho ho ho!

meaningMnemonic: A husband and his husband find a shellfish and agree to share it. Hints Picture the husbands pulling a different side of the shellfish, it pops in two, and they each get a shell. They smile and high five.
readingMnemonic: Since the husbands were able to agree , San ta-san ( さん ) believes they’re both good husbands and belong on the good list. Therefore, Santa-san gives them each lots and lots of shellfish for Christmas. Hints Imagine Santa-san flying over the husbands in his sleigh, raining shellfish down upon them from the sky. It warms the heart, wouldn’t you agree?

meaningMnemonic: You come across a spirit wearing a top hat and it claims to be your ancestor . Well of course, if you remember correctly, all of your ancestors wore top hats when they were alive. This spirit must be your long lost, great great... uh... somebody. Hints Imagine coming across your long dead top hatted ancestor in spirit form. What would you do? What would you say?
readingMnemonic: You ask your ancestor what it wants and it points to the so ap ( そ ) by the sink. Soap? It nods at you. I guess your ancestor is here to see the wonders of soap. Hints Your ancestor didn't come here to see you, it just wanted to learn about soap. Something that they didn't have back when it was alive. That's actually kinda sad... and stinky. Your ancestor needs to use this soap, if anything.

meaningMnemonic: To use your gold at the bar you need to turn it into a coin . Well, more than one coin, probably. But you know for sure that you can make at least one coin out of the gold you have. Hints Imagine yourself strenuously pushing a lever to flatten your gold and punch a coin out it. You sweat as you hurry to make enough coins so you can go to the bar before it closes.
readingMnemonic: You use the coin to pay a cen taur ( せん ) at the bar. The centaur is the bartender and he makes special drinks for those who pay in gold coins. Good for you! Hints Imagine handing this centaur bartender your gold coins. Hear him thank you in his booming voice and make you a mysterious gold-colored drink. Look in wonder at how the centaur has managed to fit in the narrow space behind the bar counter.

meaningMnemonic: If you want to go to Korea you'll need a good defense . Hints Things in Korea haven't been on the safest side lately, so make sure you have some ways to defend yourself before you go.
readingMnemonic: You need a good defense to go to Korea, so you fill your pockets with a corns ( えい ). When you get to Korea you plant them all around yourself. In no time you'll have a strong tree defense, keeping you safe. Hints Okay, so maybe this defense strategy will take a while, but you aren't rich and acorns are on the ground for free. Don't judge!

meaningMnemonic: A tree combines with a table to make a desk . When you think about it, a desk is just a table with more stuff. To make this more stuff, like drawers and such, you need more wood, and wood comes from trees. Add materials from the tree to the table and you have a desk. Hints Chop this tree into pieces to transform this table into a desk. Hear the sounds of construction in your head as you make this desk with your bare hands.
readingMnemonic: When you finish the desk you turn to your friend and say, “ It’s cool, eh ( つくえ )?” Your friend looks at you and says, “S’coo’ eh? What?” “This desk, it’s cool. It’s cool, eh?” “Aw, yeah man. S’coo’ eh.” Another way to remember this reading is to think about where you find lots of desks. That's right, in a school ( つくえ ). Hints Just imagine someone slurring “It’s cool, eh?” While you think about how cool this desk really is. Run your hands over the finished project as you say it.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami hit not one, but TWO prison s, making them extremely dirty . Hints Imagine observing the two prisons being hit by a giant wave of muddy water, making them completely dirty. How disgusting!
readingMnemonic: What's the most dirty are the prisons' o bi ( お ) collections. You can hear the prisoners crying, "Oh, not the obi. Our obi are all dirty, oh no!" Hints The obi were the only nice thing the prisoners had left, and now they're all dirty. Even as you leave the prisons, you can still hear their echoing cries of "Oh, not our obi!"

meaningMnemonic: You eat part of a director to domesticate him. This director has been going around kicking cameramen and punching actors and it’s really ruining his reputation. Hints Which part of the director did you choose to eat in order to domesticate him? Think about eating that part of the director and imagine its taste in your mouth as you chew. Eww.
readingMnemonic: While you did succeed in your attempt to domesticate the director, he is now bleeding profusely from the bite wound. All over the script! You gotta get your ca r ( か ) and drive him to the hospital like right away. Get to the car! Hurry! Hints You’re proud that you managed to domesticate the director, but now you feel kind of bad for having injured him. Okay, you really just feel bad because he’s probably going to sue you and he definitely has a lot of money. Oh, and he’s bleeding all over your car.

meaningMnemonic: If your outfit gets sucked into a black hole , you'll need to get a duplicate version of the same outfit, 'cause you're not getting the original back. Hopefully you had multiple s… Hints Always pick up a few duplicate outfits if you're planning on venturing out to a black hole.
readingMnemonic: As you're shopping for duplicate outfits, some guy runs up and starts screaming " f*** ( ふく ) you!" at you. "F*** you, man! You're out here buying multiple outfits while kids in other countries are starving!" Hints In response, you shout "F*** you too, bro! I need these duplicate outfits for my black hole mission!" For the next few minutes, the two of you just scream "f*** you" at each other multiple times, over and over.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami runs into nine tree s and produces a dye the color of the forest. See the tsunami turn from the color of water to the color of a forest. The dye washes over you and now you’re forest green as well.
readingMnemonic: The dye continues to pass through the forest and hits a group of cen taurs ( せん ). Now each centaur is dyed with the forest green dye. They don’t look happy. Hints Hear each centaur shouting about how he hates that dye for changing his color. They look kind of funny, so you laugh at them a bit, but not too loud – they might hear you and get even more angry.

meaningMnemonic: Two pool s, both altered and not quite like a pool you’ve seen before are put together and flipped around – this is an egg . readingMnemonic: You remember Tamago tchi ( たまご ), right? Well, Tamagotchi is an egg , and the toy looks like an egg, so it’s pretty easy to remember that tamago means egg. Hints Just think Tamagotchi whenever you see this kanji. Tamagotchi = tamago = egg. Easy!

meaningMnemonic: The eternity radical and the eternity kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!

readingMnemonic: How do you say cherry tree in Japanese? Sakura ( さくら ). Sakura is Japanese for cherry tree. I’m sure you’ve probably heard this before, so it shouldn’t be too hard to remember. Hints Sakura means cherry tree and sakura is the way to pronounce this kanji. Easy!

meaningMnemonic: You learned that 懐 means "nostalgia," but remember how it could also mean bosom pocket ? Well, that's what the vocab word means too: bosom pocket . 懐 originally referred to the space between the inner and outer layers of a kimono. As Western-style clothing became standard, it came to mean the inner pocket area around the chest. Since people often kept money in their 懐 , it can figuratively refer to someone's financial capacity, as seen in expressions like 懐が寒い (being short on money). It can also describe a person's capacity to be accepting and tolerant, as in 懐が深い (someone with a "deep heart pocket," meaning they are broad-minded and generous of spirit).
readingMnemonic: Your bosom pocket is the 太 core ( ふところ ) of your identity. You keep all kinds of things in there — ID cards, polaroids, mementos, a fat wad of cash — and that's why your bosom pocket looks so stuffed and 太 . Your 太 core defines you as a person, and you wouldn't be you without it!

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means deposit , and this word is for when someone is depositing something (or someone) with you, because they want you to look after , to take care of , or to hold on to it. Remember that 預ける is used when you leave something with someone else to take care of temporarily. 預かる , on the other hand, is used when you're the one receiving something to look after. You can remember this because you're great at taking care of cargo ( かる ). You're always looking after everyone's cargo, but you're happy to hold on to it for them. Also note that even though 預かる ends with かる and kind of looks intransitive, it's actually an exception! It'll pretty much always have a direct object to specify what you're looking after.
